newsitem.title: RWANDA: Refugees pile up in Rwanda as U.S. backs off force.
newsitem.headline: Refugees pile up in Rwanda as U.S. backs off force.

text.p: Huge bottle-necks of exhausted Hutu returnees built up inside Rwanda on Tuesday and the United States signalled it no longer planned to send troops for a planned multinational force for Zaire.
Rwanda again denied the force was needed because 500,000 Hutu refugees have left rebel-held eastern Zaire and returned home by foot in the past four days.
But French President Jacques Chirac and the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said the U.N.-backed force still had a vital job because 60 percent of the Rwandan Hutus are still in Zaire.
The human tide of refugees entering Rwanda from Goma, Zaire, was down to a trickle on Tuesday.
But for many Hutus the suffering continued in the homeland they fled in 1994 after their kinsmen committed genocide against minority Tutsis and pro-opposition Hutus.
Tens of thousands of returning refugees demanding food blocked the streets of Nkamira, 21 km (13 miles) from the border.
Two soldiers stood on guard outside the U.N. transit centre at Nkamira, stopping refugees from entering to have a rest, sleep and receive food as planned by the UNHCR.
Rwandan authorities insist the refugees, exhausted by days of marching and sleeping rough, keep trudging onwards to their home villages.
A spokeswoman for the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) accused Rwandan soldiers of commandeering four ICRC trucks to ferry refugees out of the crammed border area.
In Washington the Pentagon said the U.S. had tentatively decided not to send troops to Zaire and will instead use its military cargo planes to fly humanitarian aid to Rwanda.

"At one point, it looked like we needed a security component" to protect the distribution of aid to refugees in Goma, Zaire," Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon said. "Now it looks like we won't need a security component."

The U.S. was one of the most reluctant volunteers to the U.N.-backed, 10,000-strong multinational force whose confused mission was mainly to help the 1.2 million Rwandan and Burundian Hutus stranded in eastern Zaire by a month-long rebellion.
About 14 countries who committed troops to the force are due to review their plans in Germany on Thursday.
The meeting will be attended by Canadian Army Lt. General Maurice Baril, designated as commander of a force which has yet to deploy and some of whose key partners are wavering.
Baril got a pointedly low-level reception on arrival in Rwanda's capital Kigali on Tuesday.
Rwanda repeated on Tuesday the mass return meant the force was not needed and some of the money earmarked for it should be diverted to help resettle returnees.

"These refugees who have returned home number 500,000 people, which broadly matches the real number of Rwandan refugees previously in eastern Zaire, in North and South Kivu," Foreign Minister Anastase Gasana told reporters in Kigali.
Gasana's statistics contradicted the official numbers, used by all foreign governments.
The United Nations relief agency UNHCR says there were 1.1 million Rwandan Hutus and 150,000 Burundian Hutus in camps in eastern Zaire before the start of the rebellion last month.
Based on that arithmetic those arguing that the force still has a vital mission say some 600,000 refugees are scattered in Zaire, in desperate need of food, water and medicine.

"There's a big job for a multinational force to be done in eastern Zaire. Its priority should now be Bukavu (South Kivu) where there are still half a million refugees," UNHCR spokeswoman Christiane Berthiaume said in Geneva.
French President Jacques Chirac said in Tokyo the force's mandate was valid, notably to secure air fields and food convoys.

Tens of thousands of the Hutus still in Zaire are members of the former government army and Interahamwe militiamen who committed the genocide. They face execution or years in prison if they return to Rwanda.

Rwanda says those returnees with no blood on their hands have nothing to fear. But aid agencies say human rights workers must monitor the return of Hutus to villages where the houses and plantations of many of them have been occupied.
A top European official gave the mooted force an openly political mandate on Monday, saying it should also help Zaire's government against the rebels now controlling much of the east.

"The most basic of issues and the reason why I'm here today is to permit Zaire to recover total sovereignty over its territory as rapidly as possible," Aldo Ajello, a European Union envoy, told reporters in Zaire's capital Kinshasa on Monday.
This objective is brand-new and is not in the Security Council resolution authorising the multinational force.
